ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
Weeds compete directly with corn for light, water, space, and nutrients, and can significantly reduce yield if not managed, particularly during the first several weeks after crop emergence. Corn is a relatively poor competitor with weeds during this early window (commonly described as the first 3-6 weeks after emergence, sometimes called the "critical weed-free period"), so effective weed control during this specific window matters more for protecting yield than weed control later in the season, once the crop canopy has closed over and can better suppress weeds itself.

Weed pressure tends to be highest during early-wet-season plantings, when warm temperatures and good rainfall favour both the crop and weeds equally. Beyond direct competition, weeds can also provide habitat for insect pests and diseases, adding an indirect yield cost on top of the direct competition for resources.
